items.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: as a trumpet player and an arranger, I was with Hamp at 19.

ctx.x: But you don’t seem to get boxed in. Let me ask about your experiences in Hollywood, because even when you came out there, this wasn’t a norm. There were some people that delved into it, but I’m trying to think of, like, The Pawnbroker and some of the – tell me about what that was. Who were the people? Benny Carter? Who else? Earl Hagen? I don’t know.

I wanted to be in film – wanted to write for films since I was 15. I don’t know how that happened, because, as I said before, when I’ve been looking at this book and everything else, and I thought it was 15 years – I started playing trumpet ’45, 1946 or something, and it felt like this long time before I was with Hamp. It’s just, as a trumpet player and an arranger, I was with Hamp at 19. I never thought about that, because it felt like a longer period of incubation. When you look at the reality of it, it freaked…
Basically, who were the people who facilitated your getting into writing in Hollywood?

items.title: Lionel Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: And I got Quincy Jones and he was making arrangements for the band

ctx.x: So your band was like a training ground for very many young musicians.

Yeah. And later down the line I got Quincy Jones, and I almost had Ray Charles, because Quincy Jones and Ray Charles were doing gigs together in Seattle, Washington. And I got Quincy Jones and he was making arrangements for the band, and then I picked up the piano player, what was his name, oh boy, Milt Buckner. Milt Buckner. You know he plays a lot of kinds of style of piano.
Yeah. He’s a good organist too.
